title: Indian Banks Are Offering NRIs Up to 7% on Dollar Deposits. Here Is What Changed.
excerpt: HDFC Bank, SBI, and smaller lenders have hiked rates by up to 300 basis points after the RBI agreed to absorb all hedging costs. The window closes in September.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India just handed non-resident Indians a deal they haven't seen in thirteen years — and the country's biggest banks are racing to cash in.

On Wednesday, at least four major lenders announced sharp rate hikes on foreign currency deposits for NRIs, just days after the RBI said it would bear the full hedging cost on three- to five-year non-resident deposits. The move is part of a broader, increasingly urgent campaign to attract dollar inflows as the rupee slides to Asia's second-worst performing currency of 2026, down 6 per cent and touching record lows of 96.97 per dollar in May.

## What's on Offer

HDFC Bank, India's largest private sector lender, raised rates by 235 to 265 basis points, pushing its offering to 6 per cent on three- to five-year deposits. State Bank of India went further — the country's biggest bank hiked by as much as 300 basis points, now offering between 5.25 and 6 per cent depending on the deposit size and tenure. Deposits above $1 million get the top rate.

But the most aggressive plays are coming from smaller banks. AU Small Finance Bank is offering 7.1 per cent on three-year deposits and 7 per cent on five-year terms — rates that comfortably beat U.S. Treasury yields. Yes Bank has set rates at 7 to 7.1 per cent across three- to five-year tenures, according to Bloomberg.

Other banks are expected to announce their new rates this week.

## Why This Matters for NRIs

The arithmetic is straightforward. Three-year U.S. Treasuries currently yield around 4.2 per cent. A 7 per cent return on a dollar deposit — with the RBI absorbing the hedging risk — represents a significant premium over what NRIs can earn parking their money in American government bonds.

The RBI is also open to banks providing guarantees to offshore lenders who lend to NRIs, who can then place those borrowed funds as deposits. In effect, the central bank is creating an entire ecosystem designed to pull dollars out of the diaspora's savings and into India's financial system.

Punjab National Bank's CEO, Ashok Chandra, told Reuters the scheme would be marketed "aggressively" in key diaspora markets — the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and the Middle East. He estimated his bank alone would raise $2.5 to $3 billion.

Across the industry, analysts estimate the scheme could pull in $35 to $40 billion by September, when the window closes.

## The 2013 Playbook

The last time India ran a scheme like this was during the 2013 "taper tantrum," when the Fed's signalling of tighter monetary policy sent the rupee into a tailspin. Under that scheme, HDFC Bank mobilised $3.4 billion, followed by ICICI Bank, SBI and select foreign banks.

The current crisis is arguably more severe. The Iran war has disrupted global energy supplies, crude prices have hovered near $90 to $96 per barrel, and foreign portfolio investors have pulled record sums out of Indian equities. The rupee touched an all-time low of 96.97 in May before the RBI's intervention package steadied it near 95.27.

Goldman Sachs, in a note this week, said the measures "should limit the depreciation pressure on the rupee" and forecast the dollar-rupee cross at 96 in three months — down from its earlier estimate of 97. But the bank cautioned against expecting significant appreciation: "Any renewed capital inflows should and will be used to rebuild the reserve buffer."

## What NRIs Should Watch

The window is open until September 30. The key question is whether the rates hold — or whether banks compete even more aggressively as the deadline approaches. For NRIs weighing their options, the calculus is simple: India is offering a premium over U.S. yields, the RBI is absorbing the currency risk on the hedge, and the government has separately scrapped capital gains tax on foreign investments in government securities.

The risks are equally clear. If the Iran conflict deepens, oil prices spike further, and the rupee breaches 100 per dollar — a scenario some analysts have floated — the broader economic fallout could complicate returns for anyone with significant exposure to Indian assets.

For now, though, the RBI's message to the diaspora is unmistakable: bring your dollars home. India needs them.
